chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
title: The Philharmonic Hall concert and the ovation
summary: Johnson recalls the huge ovation at Charles Mingus and Friends, and young people's identification with him as a rebel.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Do you like -- this is something I've noticed. In fact, I was totally unprepared. I was standing in a corner of the stage at Philharmonic Hall, when you walked out, at that concert. And I was totally flabbergasted at the amount of applause -- I mean, not -- it literally nearly blew me off the stage, and it was an incredible ovation. And --
What concert are you talking about?
The one with the big band, the one at Philharmonic Hall.
Yeah, Lee Konitz and Mulligan and everybody. Ammons
Gene Hammonds, right, yes. And Charles Mingus and Friends at Philharmonic Hall. And the --
Yeah, that was the first time you could hear jazz concerts in a long time. That was one of the first ones.

-- stupendous ovation. And I have a feeling that part of the reason for that is that young people identify with you as a rebel. I mean, you're somebody who's earned your wings out there in the trenches, fighting for all the battles, all the things that they believe in. And aside from the music, which they really loved, too, but I think that some of the things that got you in a lot of hot water in your life earlier, that people really -- young people in particular really respect you for that.
Yeah, well, it wasn't -- the audience wasn't only young.
No, they weren't, but there were a lot of young people there.
You play a lot of colleges and young people come to hear you wherever you play.
